title: A technique spreads among peers
sourceType: Original fictional study; all participants, procedures, and numbers are invented for practice.
introduction: Researchers tracked how an existing dance technique spread among peers during a community workshop series.
participants: Seventy-one consenting dancers ages 18–45 attended the same local workshop program. Five already knew the focal technique at enrollment.
procedure: Researchers did not introduce demonstrations, assign teachers, or reward imitation. During routine sessions, observers recorded who demonstrated the technique to whom. Knowing the technique was scored as completing all four specified movement elements in a normal practice run. Weekly totals counted dancers meeting that criterion.
ethics: Dancers consented to being observed, could opt out of records, and were identified by codes rather than public names. Ordinary workshop access did not depend on participation.
resultsNote: Records included instances of one learner later demonstrating to another. The researchers observed rather than arranged these interactions.

title: Repeated pictures and a novel pattern
sourceType: Original fictional study; all participants, procedures, and numbers are invented for practice.
introduction: Researchers tested whether decreasing attention to a repeated picture would recover when a new pattern appeared.
participants: Sixty infants ages 5–7 months were recruited through one pediatric clinic with parental permission. Thirty were randomly assigned to each final-test condition.
procedure: All infants first saw the same harmless geometric picture on eight brief trials. Looking time was the number of seconds gaze stayed on the display during a 20-second window, coded from video by observers unaware of final-test assignment. At the final trial, one group saw a new pattern; the other saw the original pattern again.
ethics: Parents consented and remained with the infants. Trials stopped immediately if the infant showed distress, and families could withdraw the video from analysis.
resultsNote: The patterns were matched for size and brightness. The final manipulation concerned novelty, not a reward.

parts.label: Research method
parts.prompt: Name the research method used in this study.
parts.model: The researchers used an experiment. Final-pattern novelty was manipulated with random assignment after common repeated presentations.
criteria: Identify an experiment as the method. Design details may clarify the answer but do not replace the method name.
parts.pitfall: Random assignment is a design feature, not the name of the research method.

parts.label: Operational definition
parts.prompt: State the operational definition of looking time used in this study.
parts.model: It was the number of seconds gaze remained on the display within a 20-second trial window, as coded from video.
criteria: Give the study’s observable measurement or manipulation, including its relevant units, scoring, or time window.
parts.pitfall: A dictionary definition of the concept does not state how this particular study measured it.

parts.label: Statistic interpretation
parts.prompt: Interpret the difference between the two final-test means.
parts.model: Infants shown the new pattern looked for an average of 12 seconds versus three for the repeated pattern, a nine-second difference following the same earlier exposure.
criteria: Interpret the specified statistic accurately in the context of the measured behavior and conditions.
parts.pitfall: Name the actual variable and conditions; do not merely repeat the statistic’s value.

parts.label: Ethical guideline
parts.prompt: Identify one ethical safeguard described in the source and explain how it was used.
parts.model: Protection from harm was addressed by stopping immediately at signs of distress, while parents remained present and could withdraw the recordings.
criteria: Name a relevant ethical guideline and connect it to the specific protection reported in this study.

parts.label: Generalizability
parts.prompt: Explain how far the findings can reasonably extend beyond this sample, using a specific participant characteristic.
parts.model: Infants ages 5–7 months recruited through one clinic may not represent older children, adults, or infants from all clinical and cultural backgrounds.
criteria: Make a defensible claim about a population and justify it with an actual characteristic or sampling feature reported in the source.
parts.pitfall: Randomly assigning a convenience sample does not make it a random or representative sample of everyone.

parts.label: Argumentation
parts.prompt: Use a specific finding to explain whether the results support or challenge this claim: “A response reduced by repetition can recover when the stimulus changes.” Apply habituation and dishabituation in your explanation.
parts.model: Looking fell from 14 to three seconds across repetition, then rose to 12 for a new pattern while staying at three for the repeated one. The decline fits habituation and the novelty rebound fits dishabituation rather than a reward-based process.
criteria: For 2 points: cite an accurate, specific finding and explain how it supports or challenges the stated claim using the relevant learning mechanism.
For 1 point: a relevant result without the explanatory link, or a relevant explanatory argument without a specific result.
For 0 points: neither relevant evidence nor a defensible explanation, or a contradiction that undermines the response.
parts.pitfall: Do not call the novelty rebound spontaneous recovery: the key change is a new pattern, not merely a rest after extinction.
